subject: Hematology
front: What is the surface marker of the multipotent hematopoietic stem cell?
back: CD-34

subject: Hematology
front: What are the two main lineages arising from the multipotent hematopoietic stem cell?
back: Myeloid stem cell and lymphoid stem cell

subject: Hematology
front: What is the surface marker of the erythroblast and its PAS staining pattern?
back: CD-71; shows diffuse PAS positivity

subject: Hematology
front: What is a reticulocyte and what is its lifespan relevance?
back: An immature RBC containing residual RNA; it matures into the erythrocyte

subject: Hematology
front: What is the lifespan of a mature erythrocyte?
back: 120 days

subject: Hematology
front: What are the surface markers of the megakaryoblast?

subject: Hematology
front: What are the key features of platelets derived from megakaryocytes?
back: No nucleus (radio-resistant), lifespan of 8 days, contain dense and alpha granules

subject: Hematology
front: What is the mnemonic for dense (delta) granule contents in platelets?
back: CASH: Calcium, ADP, Serotonin, Histamine

subject: Hematology
front: Which condition is associated with absent dense granules in platelets?
back: Hermansky–Pudlak syndrome

subject: Hematology
front: What do platelet alpha granules contain?
back: Fibrinogen, fibronectin, Von Willebrand factor, and Platelet factor 4 (PF4)

subject: Hematology
front: What condition results from antibodies against platelet factor 4 (PF4)?
back: Heparin-induced thrombocytopenia (HIT)

subject: Hematology
front: Which condition is associated with absent alpha granules in platelets?
back: Gray platelet syndrome

subject: Hematology
front: What are the surface markers of the myeloblast?

subject: Hematology
front: What are the three causes of increased neutrophils listed?
back: Infection, sepsis, and leukemia (CML)

subject: Hematology
front: In what two situations are eosinophils typically increased?
back: Parasitic infections and atopic disorders

subject: Hematology
front: In which condition are basophils characteristically increased?
back: Chronic myeloid leukemia (CML)

subject: Hematology
front: What are the surface markers of the monoblast and its cytochemical stain?
back: CD-14, 64; stains positive with NSE (non-specific esterase)

subject: Hematology
front: What are the distinguishing features of a monocyte?
back: Largest circulating WBC with a kidney-shaped nucleus

subject: Hematology
front: Match the tissue macrophage to its organ: skin, liver, brain, bone.
back: Skin – Langerhans cells; Liver – Kupffer cells; Brain – Microglia; Bone – Osteoclasts

subject: Hematology
front: What markers/stains characterize the lymphoblast?
back: TdT positive, CALLA (CD-10) positive, and PAS positive with a dot/blot pattern

subject: Hematology
front: What are the distinguishing features of a lymphocyte among WBCs?
back: Smallest WBC, highest nucleus:cytoplasm ratio, and the most radiosensitive blood cell

subject: Hematology
front: What is the function and CD marker profile of B cells?
back: Mediate humoral immunity and act as antigen presenting cells (APC); CD-19, PAX5

subject: Hematology
front: What are the surface markers and morphologic features of plasma cells?
back: CD-38, 138; clock-face chromatin and a perinuclear Golgi hof

subject: Hematology
front: Which drug targets CD38 on plasma cells and in what disease is it used?
back: Daratumumab (anti-CD38); used in multiple myeloma

subject: Hematology
front: What is the function and pan marker of T cells?
back: Mediate cell-mediated immunity; pan T cell marker is CD-3

subject: Hematology
front: What is the marker of helper T cells and which MHC/cells do they interact with?
back: CD-4; interacts with MHC II found on B cells, macrophages, and dendritic cells

subject: Hematology
front: What is the marker of cytotoxic T cells and which MHC do they interact with?
back: CD-8; interacts with MHC I, present on all nucleated cells except sperm and RBCs

subject: Hematology
front: What are the markers of NK cells and their mechanism of killing?
back: CD-16, 56, 94; destroy cells lacking MHC I (tumor/viral infected cells) via the perforin-granzyme mechanism, inducing apoptosis

subject: Hematology
front: What is another name for flow cytometry and what does it detect?
back: Immunophenotyping; used to detect CD markers in leukemias/lymphomas

subject: Hematology
front: What are the two types of output from flow cytometry?
back: Scatter plot and histogram

subject: Hematology
front: What is the difference between a scatter plot and a histogram in flow cytometry?
back: A scatter plot shows two CD markers simultaneously; a histogram shows only one CD marker

subject: Hematology
front: Which cytochemical stain is used for lymphoblasts versus erythroblasts and what pattern does each show?
back: PAS stain: block/dot pattern in lymphoblasts and diffuse pattern in erythroblasts

subject: Hematology
front: Which cytochemical stain is specific for myeloblasts?
back: MPO (myeloperoxidase)

subject: Hematology
front: Which cytochemical stain is specific for monoblasts and monocytes?
back: NSE (non-specific esterase)

subject: Hematology
front: Which technique detects chromosomal abnormalities/translocations in leukemias?
back: Fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH)

subject: Hematology
front: Complete the important CD marker list: blasts and T cells.
back: Blasts – CD-34; T cells – CD-3

subject: Hematology
front: Complete the important CD marker list: B cells and helper T cells.
back: B cells – CD-19/CD-20/PAX5; Helper T cells – CD-4

subject: Hematology
front: Complete the important CD marker list: cytotoxic T cells and NK cells.
back: Cytotoxic T cells – CD-8; NK cells – CD-16/CD-56/CD-94

subject: Hematology
front: Complete the important CD marker list: myeloblast and monoblast.
back: Myeloblast – CD-13/CD-33/CD-117; Monoblast – CD-14/CD-64

subject: Hematology
front: Complete the important CD marker list: megakaryocyte and plasma cell.
back: Megakaryocyte – CD-41,42/CD-61; Plasma cell – CD-38/CD-138

subject: Hematology
front: What markers characterize the lymphoblast and what does CALLA stand for?
back: TdT/CD10; CALLA stands for Common ALL Antigen

subject: Hematology
front: On a WBC scatter plot (FSC vs SSC), how do lymphocytes appear?
back: Small cells with few granules – low FSC and low SSC

subject: Hematology
front: On a WBC scatter plot (FSC vs SSC), how do monocytes appear?
back: Larger cells with moderate complexity (intermediate FSC/SSC)

subject: Hematology
front: On a WBC scatter plot (FSC vs SSC), how do granulocytes appear?
back: Cells with many cytoplasmic granules – high SSC

subject: Hematology
front: In the example flow cytometry scatter plots shown, what four double-marker combinations are illustrated?
back: A: CD22 and TdT positive; B: CD19 and CD10 positive; C: CD34 and CD64 positive; D: CD33 and CD15 positive

subject: Hematology
front: Which specific CD marker is used as the example for a flow cytometry histogram in the notes?
back: CD45 (illustrating that a histogram displays only one CD marker at a time)

subject: Hematology
front: What is the sequence of erythroid maturation from stem cell to mature RBC?
back: Pluripotent hematopoietic stem cell → Proerythroblast (pronormoblast) → Erythroblast (normoblast) → Reticulocyte → Erythrocyte

subject: Hematology
front: What organelle changes occur during erythroid maturation?
back: The erythroblast loses its nucleus and some organelles, and the reticulocyte loses its remaining organelles to become an erythrocyte

subject: Hematology
front: How long does a reticulocyte typically spend in the marrow versus blood before becoming an erythrocyte?
back: Usually 3 days in the marrow and 1 day in the blood

subject: Hematology
front: What percentage of circulating RBCs are normally reticulocytes?
back: About 1%

subject: Hematology
front: What are the three stages of erythroblasts in order once hemoglobin synthesis starts?
back: Basophilic erythroblast → Polychromatophilic erythroblast → Orthochromatic erythroblast (early → intermediate → late)

subject: Hematology
front: Which is the first cell to show hemoglobin on electron microscopy?
back: Pro-erythroblast

subject: Hematology
front: Which is the first cell to show hemoglobin on light microscopy?
back: Polychromatophilic erythroblast

subject: Hematology
front: Which is the first erythroid cell to enter peripheral circulation?
back: The reticulocyte

subject: Hematology
front: Why are reticulocytes named as such and what stain is used to visualize them?
back: They contain a reticulum of RNA; visualized using a supravital stain (e.g. Brilliant Cresyl Blue) which also stains ribosomes

subject: Hematology
front: What is the normal reticulocyte percentage and when is it increased?
back: Normal is 0.5–1.5%; increased in hemolytic anemias

subject: Hematology
front: What is the formula for corrected reticulocyte count?
back: Corrected retic count = Retic count × (Patient's Hematocrit ÷ 45)

subject: Hematology
front: What is the formula for Reticulocyte Production Index (RPI)?
back: RPI = Corrected Retic Count ÷ Maturation Factor

subject: Hematology
front: What maturation factor is used for a hematocrit of 40% or more?

subject: Hematology
front: What maturation factor is used for a hematocrit of 30–39.9%?

subject: Hematology
front: What maturation factor is used for a hematocrit of 20–29.9%?

subject: Hematology
front: What maturation factor is used for a hematocrit below 20%?

subject: Hematology
front: What does an RPI less than 2 indicate?
back: Inadequate bone marrow response

subject: Hematology
front: What is the preferred bone marrow aspiration/biopsy site in an adult versus a child?
back: Adult – Posterior superior iliac spine (PSIS); Child – Tibia

subject: Hematology
front: Is thrombocytopenia a contraindication for bone marrow aspiration/biopsy?
back: No, it is not a contraindication; however if platelet count is under 20,000/µL, platelet transfusion is recommended before the procedure to reduce bleeding risk

subject: Hematology
front: What are the names of the needles used for bone marrow aspiration and core biopsy?
back: Salah's needle and Klima's needle for aspiration; Jamshedi's needle for core biopsy

subject: Hematology
front: At what gestational age does the yolk sac serve as the site of erythropoiesis?
back: 3–6 weeks (primitive hematopoiesis)

subject: Hematology
front: At what gestational age does the liver become the main hematopoietic site?
back: From 6 weeks onward

subject: Hematology
front: At what gestational age does the spleen begin contributing to hematopoiesis?
back: From 9 weeks onward

subject: Hematology
front: At what gestational age does bone marrow become the major hematopoietic site?
back: From 18–20 weeks onward, and it continues after birth

subject: Hematology
front: Which organ is the main fetal hematopoietic organ until late gestation and which one dominates after birth?
back: Liver is the main fetal hematopoietic organ until late gestation; bone marrow fully dominates after birth

subject: Hematology
front: Describe the temporal pattern of the alpha hemoglobin chain across life.
back: Alpha chain is present throughout life (always)

subject: Hematology
front: Describe the temporal pattern of the gamma hemoglobin chain across life.
back: Gamma chain predominates in fetal hemoglobin and disappears (goes away) in adults

subject: Hematology
front: Describe the temporal pattern of the beta hemoglobin chain across life.
back: Beta chain increases after birth

subject: Hematology
front: What is the composition and normal adult percentage of HbA1?

subject: Hematology
front: What is the composition and normal adult percentage of HbA2?

subject: Hematology
front: What is the composition and normal adult percentage of HbF?
back: α2γ2; less than 1% in adults

subject: Hematology
front: What are the HbF and HbA2 findings in beta-thalassemia minor?
back: Mild increase in HbF; HbA2 greater than 3.5%

subject: Hematology
front: What are the HbF and HbA findings in beta-thalassemia major?
back: Markedly high HbF; very low or absent HbA

subject: Hematology
front: What is the full maturation sequence of the neutrophil lineage from blast to mature cell?
back: Myeloblast → Promyelocyte → Myelocyte → Metamyelocyte → Band/stab form → Mature neutrophil

subject: Hematology
front: What characteristic feature is seen in the promyelocyte stage and in which leukemia is it increased?
back: Auer rods are seen; increased in Acute Promyelocytic Leukemia (APML)

subject: Hematology
front: What is the nuclear shape of the myelocyte stage?
back: D-shaped nucleus

subject: Hematology
front: What is the nuclear shape of the metamyelocyte stage and what mnemonic describes it?
back: Kidney-shaped nucleus, referred to as "meta-nephrons"

subject: Hematology
front: How many nuclear lobes does a mature neutrophil normally have?
back: 3–4 nuclear lobes

subject: Hematology
front: What is the LAP score and when is it performed?
back: Leukocyte Alkaline Phosphatase Score; done on left shift of the WBC lineage, i.e. presence of immature neutrophil precursors in peripheral blood

subject: Hematology
front: What is the clinical utility of the LAP score?
back: It helps differentiate a leukemoid reaction from CML

subject: Hematology
front: Is the LAP score increased or decreased in leukemoid reaction versus CML?
back: Increased in leukemoid reaction; decreased in CML (also decreased in PNH)

subject: Hematology
front: Where is the LAP enzyme located within the neutrophil?
back: In the secondary (specific) granules of mature neutrophils

subject: Hematology
front: What are toxic granules in neutrophils and when are they seen?
back: Coarse, dark azurophilic cytoplasmic granules in neutrophils, seen in severe infection/inflammation

subject: Hematology
front: What are Döhle bodies and what do they represent?
back: Pale blue cytoplasmic inclusions in neutrophils, representing dilated rough endoplasmic reticulum

subject: Hematology
front: What condition is indicated by a neutrophil with more than 5 lobes?
back: Hypersegmented neutrophil — associated with Vitamin B12/folate deficiency

subject: Hematology
front: What is the numeric criterion for calling a neutrophil hypersegmented?
back: More than 5 lobes in 5% of neutrophils or more than 6 lobes in even a single cell

subject: Hematology
front: What condition is indicated by neutrophils with fewer than 2 lobes?
back: Pelger–Huët anomaly

subject: Hematology
front: What is the significance of pseudo-Pelger–Huët cells on a peripheral smear?
back: They are a classic peripheral smear clue for Myelodysplastic Syndrome (MDS)

subject: Hematology
front: What do mast cell granules contain and what stain is used to visualize them?
back: Contain histamine; stained with toluidine blue

subject: Hematology
front: What type of reaction results from IgE-mediated mast cell degranulation?
back: Anaphylactic reaction

subject: Hematology
front: What type of reaction results from IgE-independent mast cell degranulation and what are common triggers?
back: Anaphylactoid reaction; triggers include vancomycin (red man syndrome), opioids, and radiocontrast dye

subject: Hematology
front: What are the key morphologic and lab findings in hereditary spherocytosis?
back: Loss of central pallor on the RBC and MCHC greater than 37 g/dl

subject: Hematology
front: Which mutation is most common in hereditary spherocytosis and which mutation causes the most severe presentation?
back: Ankyrin mutation is most common; presentation is most severe when associated with a Spectrin mutation

subject: Hematology
front: What is the inheritance pattern of hereditary spherocytosis?
back: Autosomal dominant (family history usually present)

subject: Hematology
front: Besides hereditary spherocytosis, what are two other causes of spherocytes on a smear?
back: AIHA (most common cause, more so in adults) and G6PD deficiency

subject: Hematology
front: What is the pathophysiologic consequence of increased osmotic fragility in hereditary spherocytosis?
back: Extravascular hemolysis, leading to splenomegaly, jaundice, and pigmented gallstones

subject: Hematology
front: What confirmatory test is used for hereditary spherocytosis and what is its mnemonic?
back: EMA (Eosin-5-Maleimide) binding test; mnemonic: "HEMA is fragile"

subject: Hematology
front: What is the treatment of choice for hereditary spherocytosis and when is it performed?
back: Splenectomy, performed after puberty

subject: Hematology
front: Which membrane protein mutation is associated with hereditary elliptocytosis?
back: Spectrin mutation

subject: Hematology
front: What is the NESTROF test and what does the acronym stand for?
back: Naked Eye Single Tube RBC Osmotic Fragility test; a bedside screening test for thalassemia

subject: Hematology
front: What is the osmotic fragility finding in thalassemia and sickle cell anemia on the NESTROF test?
back: RBCs have lower (decreased) osmotic fragility and do not lyse

subject: Hematology
front: Define osmotic fragility.
back: The susceptibility of red blood cells to hemolysis when exposed to hypotonic saline

subject: Hematology
front: In which conditions is osmotic fragility increased versus decreased?
back: Increased in hereditary spherocytosis; decreased in thalassemia and iron deficiency

subject: Hematology
front: How does mechanical fragility compare across hereditary spherocytosis, sickle cell anemia, and thalassemia?
back: Mechanical fragility is high in all of these conditions regardless of osmotic fragility differences

subject: Hematology
front: On an osmotic fragility curve, do hereditary spherocytosis cells lyse early or late compared to sickle cell anemia/thalassemia major?
back: Hereditary spherocytosis cells lyse early; sickle cell anemia and thalassemia major cells lyse late

subject: Hematology
front: What MCV value defines megaloblastic anemia?
back: MCV greater than 100 fl

subject: Hematology
front: What neutrophil finding is characteristic of megaloblastic anemia?
back: Segmented (hypersegmented) neutrophils — more than 5 lobes in 5% of cells, or more than 6 lobes in even a single cell

subject: Hematology
front: What is a Cabot ring and what does it represent?
back: A microtubule spindle remnant seen in RBCs in megaloblastic anemia

subject: Hematology
front: What skin finding is associated with Vitamin B12 deficiency?
back: Knuckle hyperpigmentation

subject: Hematology
front: What is the role of folate in DNA synthesis and how is it linked to Vitamin B12?
back: Folate is required for conversion of uracil to thymidine; Vitamin B12 is needed to regenerate active folate ("folate trap" occurs in B12 deficiency)

subject: Hematology
front: What are the hematologic consequences of folate or Vitamin B12 deficiency on the marrow?
back: Leads to pancytopenia and megaloblastic changes in the marrow; hence the reticulocyte count is low in megaloblastic anemia

subject: Hematology
front: What are causes of Vitamin B12 deficiency (per mnemonic listing)?
back: Subacute combined degeneration (SACD) association, ileal disease, pernicious anemia, gastrectomy, and being vegan

subject: Hematology
front: What are causes of folate deficiency (per mnemonic listing)?
back: Junk food diet, alcohol use, and pregnancy

subject: Hematology
front: Besides B12/folate deficiency, what two other conditions cause megaloblastic anemia?
back: UMP Synthase deficiency (associated with orotic aciduria), and Fanconi anemia (associated with bone marrow failure)

subject: Hematology
front: What combination of autoimmune conditions is termed Evans syndrome and with which leukemia is it associated?
back: AIHA + ITP is termed Evans syndrome; it is associated with CLL

subject: Hematology
front: What are target cells also called and what mnemonic lists their causes?
back: Also called codocytes; mnemonic "HALT" — Hemoglobin C, Aspleenia, Liver disease, Thalassemia

subject: Hematology
front: What are sickle cells also called and what mnemonic describes their appearance?
back: Also called drepanocytes; described as looking like a "drape silk saree"

subject: Hematology
front: What splenic finding results from repeated sickling and what RBC inclusion is seen as a consequence?
back: Autosplenectomy occurs, and Howell-Jolly bodies (nuclear remnants) are seen in asplenia

subject: Hematology
front: What is Autoimmune Hemolytic Anemia (AIHA) and how is it confirmed?
back: Hemolysis due to autoantibodies directed against RBC antigens; confirmed by a positive Direct Coombs Test (DCT), which detects antibodies on the RBC surface

subject: Hematology
front: What does the Indirect Coombs Test detect and in which clinical scenarios is it used?
back: Detects free antibodies in the serum; used in antenatal testing and cross-matching

subject: Hematology
front: In Warm AIHA, what antibody class is involved, at what temperature does it act, and what are the causes?
back: IgG antibody, acting at 37°C; caused by SLE, CLL, and drugs (beta-lactams, methyldopa)

subject: Hematology
front: What is the treatment for Warm AIHA?
back: Steroids (first line); rituximab if refractory

subject: Hematology
front: In Cold AIHA, what antibody class is involved, at what temperature does it act, and what are the causes?
back: IgM antibody, acting below 30°C; caused by Mycoplasma and EBV infection

subject: Hematology
front: What is the treatment for Cold AIHA and why are steroids not preferred?
back: Avoid cold exposure; rituximab if refractory. Steroids are usually ineffective in Cold AIHA

subject: Hematology
front: What antibody causes Paroxysmal Cold Hemoglobinuria (PCH) and against what antigen is it directed?
back: The Donath–Landsteiner antibody (IgG) directed against the P antigen of RBCs

subject: Hematology
front: What is the unique temperature behavior of the Donath–Landsteiner antibody and what type of hemolysis results?
back: It binds to RBCs at 0–4°C but causes hemolysis at 37°C, resulting in intravascular hemolysis

subject: Hematology
front: What are acanthocytes (spur cells) and what conditions are they associated with?
back: RBCs with irregular spines; associated with abetalipoproteinemia (MTTP gene), anemia of liver disease, and Vitamin E deficiency (fat malabsorption)

subject: Hematology
front: What are echinocytes (burr cells) and what conditions are they associated with?
back: RBCs with regular spines; associated with renal failure, burns, and pyruvate kinase deficiency

subject: Hematology
front: What are teardrop cells (dacrocytes) and in what conditions are they seen?
back: Teardrop-shaped RBCs seen in myelophthisis/myelofibrosis, along with a leucoerythroblastic picture and hepatosplenomegaly

subject: Hematology
front: What are helmet cells (schistocytes) and what are their microangiopathic and macroangiopathic causes?
back: Fragmented RBCs seen in MAHA; microangiopathic causes include HUS, TTP, HELLP, DIC; macroangiopathic cause is a prosthetic mitral valve

subject: Hematology
front: What is the inheritance pattern of G6PD deficiency and what is the underlying biochemical defect?
back: X-linked recessive condition; NADPH (needed for anti-oxidant action) is not formed

subject: Hematology
front: What type(s) of hemolysis occur in G6PD deficiency and what stain is used to detect it?
back: Both intravascular and extravascular hemolysis; a supravital stain is used, which stains denatured hemoglobin/RNA

subject: Hematology
front: What are bite cells also called and what causes their formation?
back: Also called degmatocytes; caused by removal of Heinz bodies (denatured hemoglobin) by splenic macrophages ('dog bites' appearance)

subject: Hematology
front: What test is used to screen for G6PD deficiency and what does it demonstrate?
back: The Fluorescent Spot Test; it demonstrates lack of NADPH fluorescence (reduced fluorescence) via the HMP shunt pathway

subject: Hematology
front: What drugs/foods precipitate oxidative hemolysis in G6PD deficiency?
back: Dapsone, sulfa drugs, primaquine, and fava beans

subject: Hematology
front: What is the underlying defect in sideroblastic anemia?
back: The heme component of hemoglobin cannot be formed properly

subject: Hematology
front: Where does iron accumulate in sideroblastic anemia and what is this finding called on bone marrow exam?
back: Iron accumulates in mitochondria around the nucleus of erythroblasts, seen as ring sideroblasts in the bone marrow

subject: Hematology
front: What are the three causes of sideroblastic anemia?
back: ALA Synthase deficiency (X-linked recessive condition), Vitamin B6 deficiency (cofactor for ALA synthase; can be caused by INH/isoniazid), and lead poisoning (inhibits ALA dehydratase and Ferrochelatase)

subject: Hematology
front: What smear finding is described as coarse basophilic stippling and what stain highlights iron-related inclusions in sideroblastic anemia?
back: Basophilic stippling is a coarse granular pattern in RBCs; Perl's/Prussian blue stain highlights iron deposits (ringed sideroblasts, Pappenheimer bodies)

subject: Hematology
front: What are the hemoglobin cut-offs defining anemia in men, women, and pregnancy?
back: Male: less than 13 g/dL; Female: less than 12 g/dL; Pregnancy: less than 11 g/dL

subject: Hematology
front: How is anemia classified based on MCV and what are the cut-offs?
back: Microcytic (MCV less than 80 fl), Normocytic (MCV 80–100 fl), Macrocytic (MCV greater than 100 fl)

subject: Hematology
front: What is the mnemonic SITA for causes of microcytic anemia?
back: Sideroblastic anemia, Iron deficiency anemia (IDA), Thalassemia, Anemia of chronic disease (AOCD)

subject: Hematology
front: Within normocytic anemia, how are hemolytic and non-hemolytic anemia distinguished by reticulocyte response?
back: Hemolytic anemia shows an increased/compensatory reticulocyte count (typically >2%); non-hemolytic anemia shows a normal or low reticulocyte index

subject: Hematology
front: What are the four listed causes of non-hemolytic normocytic anemia?
back: Aplastic anemia, CKD (due to EPO deficiency), Anemia of chronic disease (AOCD), and early iron deficiency

subject: Hematology
front: What are the three categories of membrane defects causing intrinsic (RBC defect) hemolytic anemia and their inheritance?
back: Hereditary spherocytosis (AD), Hereditary elliptocytosis (AD), and PNH (acquired)

subject: Hematology
front: What are the two enzyme defects causing intrinsic hemolytic anemia and their inheritance?
back: G6PD deficiency (X-linked recessive) and Pyruvate kinase deficiency (autosomal recessive)

subject: Hematology
front: What are the three hemoglobinopathies causing intrinsic hemolytic anemia and their inheritance?
back: Sickle cell disease (AR), Hemoglobin C disease (AR), and Thalassemia (AR)

subject: Hematology
front: What are the two categories of extrinsic hemolytic anemia and their causes?
back: Immune (AIHA) and Mechanical/Microangiopathic (MAHA)

subject: Hematology
front: What lab findings characterize intravascular hemolysis and what are its causes?
back: Markedly increased LDH, markedly decreased haptoglobin, and hemoglobinuria; caused by PNH and MAHA

subject: Hematology
front: What lab and clinical findings characterize extravascular hemolysis and where does it occur?
back: Occurs in macrophages of the spleen/liver; findings include mild-moderately increased LDH, increased unconjugated bilirubin, splenomegaly, and pigment gallstones; caused by every other cause of hemolytic anemia

subject: Hematology
front: Which two conditions show features of both intravascular and extravascular hemolysis?
back: G6PD deficiency and Sickle cell disease

subject: Hematology
front: What are the four listed causes of megaloblastic macrocytic anemia?
back: Vitamin B12 deficiency, Folate deficiency, Orotic aciduria (UMP Synthase deficiency), and Fanconi anemia

subject: Hematology
front: What are the five listed causes of non-megaloblastic macrocytic anemia?
back: Alcohol use, Hypothyroidism, Aplastic anemia, Reticulocytosis, and Diamond-Blackfan anemia

subject: Hematology
front: What is the underlying defect in Fanconi anemia and what are its key clinical features?
back: A DNA repair defect; features include pancytopenia, short stature, café-au-lait macules, and radial ray abnormalities (absent or hypoplastic radius/thumb)

subject: Hematology
front: What are the key clinical features of Diamond-Blackfan syndrome?
back: Pure red cell aplasia, triphalangeal thumb, craniofacial anomalies, and presentation in infancy

subject: Hematology
front: Besides aplastic anemia, CKD, AOCD, and early iron deficiency, what other entity is listed as a cause of non-hemolytic normocytic anemia?
back: Pure Red Cell Aplasia (PRCA)

subject: Hematology
front: Describe the pathway of dietary iron absorption from gut lumen to storage.
back: Dietary Fe3+ is reduced to Fe2+ by intestinal enzymes, enters via DMT-1, is exported out of the enterocyte via ferroportin (inhibited by hepcidin), transferred in blood as transferrin, and stored as ferritin

subject: Hematology
front: What is the pathophysiology of iron overload in hereditary hemochromatosis?
back: Mutation in the HFE gene leads to inadequate hepcidin production, so ferroportin remains active, causing excess iron absorption from the intestine and progressive iron overload

subject: Hematology
front: How does serum iron differ across IDA, AOCD, sideroblastic anemia, and OCP use?
back: IDA: decreased (iron stores depleted); AOCD: decreased (iron trapped in macrophages); Sideroblastic anemia: increased; OCP use: normal

subject: Hematology
front: How does transferrin/TIBC differ across IDA, AOCD, sideroblastic anemia, and OCP use?
back: IDA: increased (hungry for more iron); AOCD: decreased (not hungry for iron); Sideroblastic anemia: decreased; OCP use: markedly increased

subject: Hematology
front: How does ferritin (an acute phase reactant) differ across IDA, AOCD, sideroblastic anemia, and OCP use?
back: IDA: decreased (iron stores depleted); AOCD: increased (acute phase reactant); Sideroblastic anemia: increased; OCP use: normal

subject: Hematology
front: How does transferrin saturation differ across IDA, AOCD, sideroblastic anemia, and OCP use?
back: IDA: markedly decreased (no iron to bind); AOCD: decreased (circulating iron is low); Sideroblastic anemia: markedly increased; OCP use: decreased

subject: Hematology
front: What is the Mentzer index formula and its cutoff to distinguish IDA from thalassemia minor?
back: Mentzer index = MCV divided by RBC count; less than 13 suggests thalassemia minor, greater than 13 suggests IDA

subject: Hematology
front: How does RDW differ between IDA and thalassemia minor?
back: RDW is increased in IDA and low (normal) in thalassemia minor

subject: Hematology
front: What is the confirmatory test for thalassemia and what HbA2/HbF findings support thalassemia minor versus major?
back: HPLC is the confirmatory test; HbA2 is increased (greater than 2%) in thalassemia minor, while HbF is increased in thalassemia major

subject: Hematology
front: What is considered the best test to definitively confirm thalassemia?
back: DNA sequencing

subject: Hematology
front: How many alpha-globin genes are normally present and on which chromosome are they located?
back: 4 alpha-globin genes total (2 on each copy of chromosome 16)

subject: Hematology
front: What is the clinical picture with a single alpha-globin allele deletion?
back: Alpha-thalassemia minima — asymptomatic

subject: Hematology
front: What is the clinical picture with two alpha-globin allele deletions?
back: Alpha-thalassemia minor — mild anemia (IDA-like)

subject: Hematology
front: What is the clinical picture with three alpha-globin allele deletions?
back: HbH disease — severe anemia, splenomegaly, and formation of β4 hemoglobin producing golf ball inclusions

subject: Hematology
front: What is the clinical picture with four alpha-globin allele deletions?
back: Hb Bart's disease — Hb Bart's is γ4 tetramer, causing hydrops fetalis and intrauterine death (mnemonic: "Bart – no birth")

subject: Hematology
front: How many beta-globin genes are normally present and where is the defect located in beta thalassemia?
back: 2 beta-globin genes present; caused by a splicing defect on chromosome 11

subject: Hematology
front: What is the clinical picture of beta-thalassemia minor (trait)?
back: One abnormal allele plus one normal allele; causes mild anemia (IDA-like) with increased HbA2

subject: Hematology
front: What is the clinical picture of beta-thalassemia major (Cooley's anemia)?
back: Both beta-globin alleles are abnormal or absent, causing severe anemia with increased HbF, jaundice, hepatosplenomegaly, and transfusion dependence

subject: Hematology
front: What radiologic and facial findings are classically seen in beta-thalassemia major?
back: "Hair on end" skull X-ray appearance, chipmunk facies, and mediastinal extramedullary hematopoiesis

subject: Hematology
front: Which specific beta-globin splicing mutation is noted as most common in India?
back: The IVS1-5 G→C splicing mutation

subject: Hematology
front: What is the approximate normal value for transferrin saturation?
back: Approximately 33%

subject: Hematology
front: On hemoglobin electrophoresis, what pattern is seen in a normal adult (AA) versus a normal newborn (AF)?
back: AA shows normal adult hemoglobin; AF shows normal newborn hemoglobin (HbF, α2γ2), which has more affinity for O2

subject: Hematology
front: What are the electrophoresis patterns and clinical associations of AS, SS, AC, CC, and SC genotypes?
back: AS: sickle cell trait (risk of medullary RCC, protective against malaria); SS: sickle cell anemia; AC: hemoglobin C trait; CC: hemoglobin C disease; SC: hemoglobin S-C disease

subject: Hematology
front: What is the composition and normal adult percentage of HbA1 and HbA2 (per hemoglobin electrophoresis notes)?
back: HbA1 (α2β2) is about 90% of adult Hb; HbA2 (α2δ2) is 2–5% of adult Hb, and is raised in thalassemia minor

subject: Hematology
front: What point mutation causes sickle cell anemia and what is the mnemonic for it?
back: Glutamate is replaced by Valine; mnemonic: "Glutamate go, Valine welcome"

subject: Hematology
front: What point mutation causes Hemoglobin C disease and what is the mnemonic for it?
back: Glutamate is replaced by Lysine; mnemonic: "Ly'C'ine"

subject: Hematology
front: What mnemonic helps recall the order of hemoglobin bands (C, S, F, A) from the origin on electrophoresis?
back: "A Fat Santa Clause" — read in reverse order (Clause, Santa, Fat, A) it gives C, S, F, A, the migration order from the origin

subject: Hematology
front: What are the precipitating factors for sickle cell crises and their pathophysiologic effect?
back: Hypoxia and acidosis, which cause RBC sickling and microvascular occlusion

subject: Hematology
front: What is the metabisulfite test used for in sickle cell disease?
back: It is a screening test that creates a hypoxic environment to demonstrate RBC sickling

subject: Hematology
front: What are the vaso-occlusive crisis manifestations of sickle cell disease?
back: Dactylitis (hand-foot syndrome), priapism, acute chest syndrome, avascular necrosis (especially of the femoral head), stroke, and renal papillary necrosis

subject: Hematology
front: What are the treatment options for sickle cell disease and their mechanisms?
back: Hydroxyurea (increases HbF), Voxelotor (increases Hb affinity for O2), Crizanlizumab (P-selectin inhibitor), and supportive care (hydration, analgesics, oxygen)

subject: Hematology
front: What is the normal function of CD55 and CD59 on RBCs?
back: They prevent complement-mediated destruction of RBCs (CD59 is also known as MIRL)

subject: Hematology
front: What is the molecular defect in Paroxysmal Nocturnal Hemoglobinuria (PNH)?
back: Inactivation of CD55 and CD59 due to a PIGA gene mutation affecting the GPI anchor

subject: Hematology
front: What triggers hemolysis in PNH and by what mechanism?
back: Reduced pH at night causes complement-mediated intravascular lysis of RBCs

subject: Hematology
front: What hematologic malignancies/conditions is PNH associated with?
back: Both pancytopenia and (rarely) leukemia

subject: Hematology
front: What thrombotic complication is PNH associated with and what is its significance?
back: Thrombosis, including Budd-Chiari syndrome, which is the most common cause of death in PNH

subject: Hematology
front: What are the screening tests for PNH?
back: Ham's acidified serum test, sucrose lysis test, and Gel Card test

subject: Hematology
front: What is the investigation of choice for diagnosing PNH?
back: Flow cytometry / FLAER

subject: Hematology
front: What is the treatment for PNH and what prophylaxis is required?
back: Eculizumab or Ravulizumab (C5 inhibitors); prophylaxis against encapsulated organisms is required

subject: Hematology
front: What are the two main branch points in the approach to pancytopenia?
back: Presence or absence of hepatosplenomegaly (HSM), and whether the marrow is hypercellular or shows a dry tap

subject: Hematology
front: In pancytopenia with hepatosplenomegaly, what does a hypercellular marrow versus a dry tap suggest?
back: Hypercellular marrow suggests leukemia; a dry tap suggests myelofibrosis

subject: Hematology
front: What are the WHO and FAB blast percentage criteria for diagnosing leukemia?
back: WHO classification: 20% or more blasts in bone marrow or peripheral blood; FAB classification: 30% or more blasts

subject: Hematology
front: What are the characteristic bone marrow/smear findings in myelofibrosis?
back: Bone marrow infiltration, a leukoerythroblastic picture, and tear drop cells (dacrocytes)

subject: Hematology
front: What drives fibrosis in myelofibrosis and what stain confirms it?
back: TGF-β stimulates fibroblast proliferation leading to marrow fibrosis, confirmed using a reticulin stain

subject: Hematology
front: What symptom is classically caused by the hepatosplenomegaly of myelofibrosis/leukemia?
back: A dragging sensation in the abdomen

subject: Hematology
front: In pancytopenia without hepatosplenomegaly, what does a hypercellular marrow versus a dry tap suggest?
back: Hypercellular marrow suggests myelodysplasia (MDS); a dry tap suggests aplastic anemia

subject: Hematology
front: What are the characteristic bone marrow findings in myelodysplastic syndrome (MDS)?
back: Pawn ball megakaryocytes and pseudo Pelger-Huët cells

subject: Hematology
front: What is the blast percentage cutoff in MDS and what mutations are commonly associated with it?
back: Marrow blasts are less than 20%, with defined mutations including 5q deletion (seen in elderly patients), SF3B1, and p53; monosomy of chromosome 7 is most common in children

subject: Hematology
front: How do primary MDS and therapy-related MDS differ in course and prognosis?
back: Primary MDS is seen in the elderly and develops slowly; therapy-related MDS occurs after chemotherapy/radiotherapy and has a poor prognosis

subject: Hematology
front: What is the risk of progression to AML in MDS?
back: About 50%

subject: Hematology
front: What is the characteristic bone marrow finding that defines aplastic anemia?
back: More than 50% fat cells in the bone marrow

subject: Hematology
front: What is the congenital cause of aplastic anemia and what causes pure red cell aplasia?
back: Fanconi anemia is the congenital cause of aplastic anemia; Parvovirus B19 causes pure red cell aplasia

subject: Hematology
front: What is the most common cause of agranulocytosis and what other causes of aplastic anemia are listed?
back: Drug toxicity is the most common cause of agranulocytosis; other causes of aplastic anemia include viral infections (EBV, HIV, hepatitis) and radiation

subject: Hematology
front: What are the two major divisions of leukemia based on clinical course?
back: Chronic leukemia and Acute leukemia

subject: Hematology
front: What are the two types of chronic leukemia based on cell lineage and what mnemonics describe their typical patient/smear appearance?
back: CLL (lymphocytic, described as a "convent school girl" appearance) and CML (myeloid, described as a "college party/garden party" appearance)

subject: Hematology
front: What are the key epidemiologic and cytogenetic features of CLL?
back: Most common leukemia in adults and Western countries; associated with 13q deletion; not associated with radiation exposure

subject: Hematology
front: What smear finding is characteristic of CLL and is it a true finding or artefact?
back: Smudge cells — a processing artefact seen on smear

subject: Hematology
front: What staging system is used for CLL?
back: Binet or Rai staging

subject: Hematology
front: What is the investigation of choice for CLL/all NHL and the treatment for CLL?
back: Flow cytometry is the investigation of choice; Fludarabine is the treatment

subject: Hematology
front: What is the classic clinical hallmark of CML?
back: Massive splenomegaly

subject: Hematology
front: What is the Philadelphia chromosome and its molecular weight/fusion gene in CML?
back: t(9;22), 210 kD, also known as t(BCR:ABL)

subject: Hematology
front: Which signaling pathway is activated in CML?
back: JAK-STAT pathway

subject: Hematology
front: What characteristic cells are seen on bone marrow in CML?
back: Pseudo-Gaucher cells

subject: Hematology
front: What is the investigation of choice and treatment for CML?
back: IOC: FISH for t(9;22); Treatment: Tyrosine kinase inhibitors (Imatinib, Dasatinib)

subject: Hematology
front: What are the two types of acute leukemia by age predominance and what is the predominant blast cell type in each?
back: ALL predominantly affects children (lymphoblasts); AML predominantly affects adults (myeloblasts)

subject: Hematology
front: What are the diagnostic markers/stains for ALL?
back: TdT positive, CALLA (CD10) positive, and PAS stain showing a dot-blot pattern

subject: Hematology
front: What are the diagnostic markers/stains for AML?
back: CD-13, CD-33, CD-117; positive for MPO and Sudan Black B

subject: Hematology
front: What are the poor prognostic factors in ALL?
back: Age less than 1 year or greater than 10 years; t(9;22)-190kD; T-cell type (with brain/testes/mediastinum involvement); L2 or L3 morphology

subject: Hematology
front: What are the good prognostic factors in ALL?
back: Pre-B cell type; L1 morphology; hyperdiploidy; and t(12;21)

subject: Hematology
front: Which leukemia is most common in children and in Down syndrome overall?
back: Acute Lymphoblastic Leukemia (ALL) for both

subject: Hematology
front: Which leukemia is most common in Down syndrome patients under 3 years of age?
back: AML-M7 (acute megakaryoblastic leukemia)

subject: Hematology
front: Which leukemia is most common in adults and with radiation exposure?
back: Acute Myeloid Leukemia (AML) for both

subject: Hematology
front: Which leukemia is most common in the elderly and in Western countries?
back: Chronic Lymphocytic Leukemia (CLL) for both

subject: Hematology
front: Which leukemia is NOT associated with radiation and which is associated with deletion of 13q?
back: CLL is not associated with radiation and is the leukemia associated with deletion of 13q

subject: Hematology
front: What are the three phases of Chronic Myeloid Leukemia (CML)?
back: Chronic phase, Accelerated phase, and Blast crisis (blast phase)

subject: Hematology
front: What are the diagnostic criteria for the accelerated phase of CML?
back: Blasts 15–30% in blood or bone marrow, persistent thrombocytopenia (less than 100,000) unrelated to therapy, basophils ≥20% in peripheral blood, splenomegaly unresponsive to therapy, and clonal evolution while on therapy

subject: Hematology
front: What are the diagnostic criteria for blast phase (blast crisis) of CML?
back: Blasts ≥20% in blood or bone marrow with extramedullary proliferation

subject: Hematology
front: What defines AML subtype M0 in the WHO-FAB classification?
back: Undifferentiated acute myeloid leukemia

subject: Hematology
front: What defines AML subtype M1?
back: Immature AML with minimal granulocytic differentiation

subject: Hematology
front: What defines AML subtype M2 and what cytogenetic abnormality is associated with it?
back: AML with granulocytic differentiation; presents as chloroma; most commonly associated with t(8;21); MPO positive

subject: Hematology
front: What defines AML subtype M3 (APML) including its cytogenetics, complication, and treatment?
back: Acute Promyelocytic Leukemia; associated with DIC and t(15;17) (PML-RARA fusion); treated with ATRA (All-Trans Retinoic Acid)

subject: Hematology
front: What defines AML subtypes M4 and M5?
back: M4 is associated with inv(16) and gum infiltration; M5 also shows gum infiltration; both are monocytic subtypes (NSE positive) and can cause leukemia cutis

subject: Hematology
front: What defines AML subtype M6?
back: Erythroblastic leukemia; CD71 positive, PAS diffusely positive

subject: Hematology
front: What defines AML subtype M7 and what syndrome is it associated with?
back: Acute megakaryoblastic leukemia; associated with Down syndrome and a dry tap on bone marrow aspiration

subject: Hematology
front: What are Faggot cells and in which leukemia are they seen?
back: Cells containing bundles of Auer rods; seen in Acute Promyelocytic Leukemia (APML)

subject: Hematology
front: What is differentiation syndrome and which drug causes it?
back: A side effect of ATRA (used for APML) presenting with fever and bilateral lung infiltrates; treated with steroids (drug of choice)

subject: Hematology
front: What is the classic clinical presentation of hairy cell leukemia?
back: Splenomegaly with pancytopenia

subject: Hematology
front: What bone marrow finding and cytochemical stain are characteristic of hairy cell leukemia?
back: A dry tap on bone marrow aspiration, and a positive TRAP (tartrate-resistant acid phosphatase) stain

subject: Hematology
front: Which gene mutation is associated with hairy cell leukemia?
back: BRAF mutation

subject: Hematology
front: What are the immunohistochemical markers of hairy cell leukemia?
back: Annexin A1 (most specific and sensitive) and CD11c, CD25, CD103

subject: Hematology
front: What is Annexin V a marker of, in contrast to Annexin A1?
back: Annexin V is a marker for apoptosis (not specific to hairy cell leukemia like Annexin A1)

subject: Hematology
front: Which part of the spleen does hairy cell leukemia affect and what infection is associated with it?
back: Affects the red pulp of the spleen; associated with MAC (Mycobacterium avium complex) infections

subject: Hematology
front: What is the drug of choice for hairy cell leukemia?
back: Cladribine

subject: Hematology
front: What five conditions classically show a 'fried-egg' appearance?
back: Hairy cell leukemia (on bone marrow biopsy), Oligodendroglioma (with 1p/19q codeletion), Seminoma/Dysgerminoma, Mycoplasma pneumoniae (colonies on culture), and Malassezia furfur (yeast on microscopy)

subject: Hematology
front: Besides ATRA, what other drug is used in the treatment of APML (AML M3) and what is ATRA's approximate success rate?
back: Arsenic trioxide (As2O3) is also used; ATRA achieves approximately 90% success/response rate

subject: Hematology
front: How does lymph node involvement typically differ between Hodgkin Lymphoma (HL) and Non-Hodgkin Lymphoma (NHL)?
back: HL typically involves a single axial group of nodes (most commonly post-cervical); NHL typically involves multiple lymph node groups

subject: Hematology
front: How does the pattern of spread differ between HL and NHL?
back: HL spreads in an orderly fashion by contiguity; NHL spreads in a non-contiguous pattern

subject: Hematology
front: What are the common nodal sites for HL versus NHL?
back: HL mainly involves cervical/mediastinal nodes; NHL commonly involves mesenteric nodes and the Waldeyer ring

subject: Hematology
front: How common is extranodal involvement in HL versus NHL?
back: Rare in HL; very common in NHL

subject: Hematology
front: How does the prognosis compare between HL and NHL?
back: HL generally has a better prognosis; NHL generally has a worse prognosis

subject: Hematology
front: What is the standard chemotherapy regimen for Hodgkin Lymphoma and what does the acronym stand for?
back: ABVD: Adriamycin, Bleomycin, Vinblastine, Dacarbazine

subject: Hematology
front: What is the standard chemotherapy regimen for Non-Hodgkin Lymphoma and what does the acronym stand for?
back: R-CHOP: Rituximab, Cyclophosphamide, Doxorubicin, Vincristine, Prednisone

subject: Hematology
front: What staging system is used for both HL and NHL?
back: Modified Ann Arbor staging (Cotswolds staging)

subject: Hematology
front: What defines Ann Arbor Stage I lymphoma?
back: A single lymph node region or a single extralymphatic organ (IE)

subject: Hematology
front: What defines Ann Arbor Stage II lymphoma?
back: Two or more lymph node regions on the same side of the diaphragm

subject: Hematology
front: What defines Ann Arbor Stage III lymphoma?
back: Lymph nodes involved on both sides of the diaphragm

subject: Hematology
front: What defines Ann Arbor Stage IV lymphoma?
back: Diffuse or disseminated extranodal involvement (e.g. bone marrow, liver)

subject: Hematology
front: What does the special suffix "B" indicate in Ann Arbor staging and what does it comprise?
back: Presence of B symptoms (constitutional symptoms): fever, night sweats, and unintentional weight loss

subject: Hematology
front: What does the special suffix "X" indicate in Ann Arbor staging?
back: Presence of bulky disease

subject: Hematology
front: What is Pel-Ebstein fever and in which lymphoma is it classically seen?
back: A cyclical fever pattern (1 week of fever followed by 1 week afebrile), classically seen in Hodgkin Lymphoma

subject: Hematology
front: Which translocations are associated with Burkitt lymphoma and which gene do they involve?
back: t(8;14), t(8;22), and t(2;8), all involving the C-myc gene on chromosome 8 (mnemonic: 8≈B for Burkitt)

subject: Hematology
front: Which translocation involving chromosome 8 is an exception and NOT associated with Burkitt lymphoma?
back: t(8;21), which is instead associated with AML M2

subject: Hematology
front: Which translocation is associated with marginal zone lymphoma and what genes does it involve?
back: t(11;18), involving genes related to marginal zone lymphoma (mnemonic: "takes margins")

subject: Hematology
front: Which translocation is associated with mantle cell lymphoma and what is its mnemonic?
back: t(11;14), involving Cyclin D1 and IgH (mnemonic: "ends with El: Eleven")

subject: Hematology
front: Which translocation is associated with follicular lymphoma and what is its mnemonic?
back: t(14;18), involving IgH and BCL-2 (mnemonic: "follicular, fourteen")

subject: Hematology
front: Along the B-cell germinal center differentiation pathway, which lymphoma arises from naive/mantle zone B cells?
back: CLL/SLL (from naive B cells) and Mantle cell lymphoma (from mantle zone B cells)

subject: Hematology
front: Which lymphomas arise from germinal center B cells?
back: DLBCL, Burkitt lymphoma, and Follicular lymphoma

subject: Hematology
front: Which lymphoma arises from marginal zone memory B cells and which malignancy arises from plasma B cells?
back: Marginal zone lymphoma arises from marginal zone memory B cells; Multiple myeloma arises from plasma B cells

subject: Hematology
topic: Approach to B-Cell and T-Cell NHL
front: Which CD marker confirms B-cell origin in the NHL approach algorithm?
back: CD19/CD20 positivity

subject: Hematology
topic: Approach to B-Cell and T-Cell NHL
front: If CD5 and CD23 are both positive in a B-cell NHL workup, what is the diagnosis and its associated findings?
back: SLL/CLL; associated with 13q deletion and Evans syndrome (AIHA + ITP); smudge cells seen on smear

subject: Hematology
topic: Approach to B-Cell and T-Cell NHL
front: If CD5 is positive and CD23 is negative in a B-cell NHL workup, what is the diagnosis and its markers/morphology?
back: Mantle cell lymphoma; positive for Cyclin D1 and SOX11, with "cleaved/buttock" cell morphology and association with lymphomatoid polyposis

subject: Hematology
topic: Approach to B-Cell and T-Cell NHL
front: If both CD5 and CD23 are negative in a B-cell NHL workup, what is the diagnosis and its associations?
back: Marginal zone lymphoma; associated with MALTOMA and other chronic inflammatory conditions

subject: Hematology
topic: Approach to B-Cell and T-Cell NHL
front: What does CD10 positivity indicate in the B-cell NHL workup?
back: It indicates actively dividing cells

subject: Hematology
topic: Approach to B-Cell and T-Cell NHL
front: If CD10 and BCL-6 are positive, what is the diagnosis and its key features?
back: Diffuse Large B-Cell Lymphoma (DLBCL); it is the most common NHL, an aggressive tumor, and is associated with EBV

subject: Hematology
topic: Approach to B-Cell and T-Cell NHL
front: What is Richter transformation?
back: Transformation of CLL/SLL into DLBCL

subject: Hematology
topic: Approach to B-Cell and T-Cell NHL
front: If CD10 and BCL-2 are positive, what is the diagnosis, its prognosis, and clinical course?
back: Follicular lymphoma; has the best prognosis among NHLs (mnemonic: "2 good to be true"), with waxing and waning lymphadenopathy

subject: Hematology
topic: Approach to B-Cell and T-Cell NHL
front: What is the aggressiveness and driver gene of Burkitt lymphoma?
back: Most aggressive NHL (Ki-67 nearly 100%), driven by the C-Myc gene

subject: Hematology
topic: Approach to B-Cell and T-Cell NHL
front: What are the endemic and sporadic clinical presentations of Burkitt lymphoma?
back: Endemic type presents with jaw swelling and is associated with EBV (seen in Africa); sporadic type presents with an abdominal mass

subject: Hematology
topic: Approach to B-Cell and T-Cell NHL
front: What histologic pattern is characteristic of Burkitt lymphoma and what do the components represent?
back: "Starry sky" appearance — the background represents tumor cells and the "stars" represent macrophages

subject: Hematology
topic: Approach to B-Cell and T-Cell NHL
front: What special stain is used on Burkitt lymphoma cells?
back: Oil red O

subject: Hematology
topic: Approach to B-Cell and T-Cell NHL
front: Which CD marker confirms T-cell origin in the NHL approach algorithm?
back: CD3 positivity

subject: Hematology
topic: Approach to B-Cell and T-Cell NHL
front: What causes Adult T-Cell Leukemia/Lymphoma (ATLL) and what is its hallmark cell?
back: Caused by HTLV-1 (Human T-cell Lymphotropic Virus, a retrovirus) infection; hallmark cell is the flower cell (cloverleaf nucleus)

subject: Hematology
topic: Approach to B-Cell and T-Cell NHL
front: What is the hallmark cell and markers of Anaplastic Large Cell Lymphoma (ALCL)?
back: Hallmark cell is the "donut cell"; positive for CD30 and ALK

subject: Hematology
topic: Approach to B-Cell and T-Cell NHL
front: Besides ALCL, what other conditions can show ALK positivity?
back: Neuroblastoma, adenocarcinoma of the lung, and inflammatory pseudotumor

subject: Hematology
topic: Approach to B-Cell and T-Cell NHL
front: What is Mycosis Fungoides and what is it called when disseminated in the blood?
back: A type of cutaneous T-cell lymphoma; when disseminated into the blood it is called Sezary syndrome

subject: Hematology
topic: Approach to B-Cell and T-Cell NHL
front: What are the key histologic features of Mycosis Fungoides?
back: Epidermotropism (T cells migrating into the epidermis) and a cerebriform nucleus (brain-like nuclear folds)

subject: Hematology
topic: Approach to B-Cell and T-Cell NHL
front: What is a Pautrier microabscess?
back: A cluster of malignant T cells within the epidermis — a special finding in Mycosis Fungoides

subject: Hematology
front: What are the two main categories of Hodgkin Lymphoma?
back: Nodular Lymphocyte Predominant Hodgkin Lymphoma (NLPHL) and Classical Hodgkin Lymphoma

subject: Hematology
front: What are the immunohistochemical markers of Nodular Lymphocyte Predominant HL?
back: CD20 positive, CD45 positive, EMA positive, BCL-6 positive, and EBV LMP negative

subject: Hematology
front: What is the characteristic cell of NLPHL and what is its prognosis?
back: L&H type Reed-Sternberg cells, also called popcorn cells; rare and carries the best prognosis (mnemonic: "Predominant – popcorn")

subject: Hematology
front: What are the immunohistochemical markers of Classical Hodgkin Lymphoma?
back: CD15 positive, CD30 positive (most sensitive), and PAX5 positive (most specific); associated with EBV (EBV LMP positive)

subject: Hematology
front: What mnemonic helps recall the two classic markers of classical HL?
back: "15 x 2 = 30" — recalling CD15 and CD30 as the classic markers

subject: Hematology
front: What are the four histologic subtypes of Classical Hodgkin Lymphoma?
back: Nodular Sclerosis, Mixed Cellularity, Lymphocyte Rich, and Lymphocyte Depleted

subject: Hematology
front: What is the characteristic RS cell, background feature, and frequency of Nodular Sclerosis HL?
back: Lacunar RS cells with collagen bands/nodules dividing the tissue; it is the most common subtype of Hodgkin Lymphoma overall

subject: Hematology
front: What is the characteristic RS cell and background of Mixed Cellularity HL,  and where is it most common?
back: Classic (eosinophilic) RS cell with a mixed inflammatory background; most common subtype in India

subject: Hematology
front: What is the characteristic RS cell, background, and prognosis of Lymphocyte Rich HL?
back: Mono-nuclear RS cell with a lymphocytic background; carries the best prognosis among classical HL subtypes (mnemonic: "rich is good prognosis")

subject: Hematology
front: What is the characteristic RS cell, rarity, and prognosis of Lymphocyte Depleted HL?
back: Mummified RS cells; the rarest subtype and carries the worst prognosis

subject: Hematology
front: What are the plasma cell percentage, M protein level, and CRAB status that define Multiple Myeloma?
back: Plasma cells ≥10%, M protein ≥3 g/dL, and CRAB features present (Yes)

subject: Hematology
front: What are the plasma cell percentage, M protein level, and CRAB status that define Smoldering (evolving) Multiple Myeloma?
back: Plasma cells ≥10%, M protein ≥3 g/dL, but CRAB features absent (No)

subject: Hematology
front: What are the plasma cell percentage, M protein level, and CRAB status that define MGUS?
back: Plasma cells less than 10%, M protein less than 3 g/dL, and CRAB features absent (No)

subject: Hematology
front: What are the plasma cell percentage, M protein level, and CRAB status that define Plasma Cell Leukemia?
back: Plasma cells ≥20%, M protein variable, and CRAB features severe

subject: Hematology
front: What type of monoclonal gammopathy is Waldenström Macroglobulinemia and which gene mutation is implicated?
back: IgM monoclonal gammopathy; associated with a MYD88 mutation

subject: Hematology
front: What are the clinical features of Waldenström Macroglobulinemia?
back: Hyperviscosity (headache, blurred vision), neuropathy, lymphadenopathy, and hepatosplenomegaly; no lytic bone lesions occur

subject: Hematology
front: What does the "C" in CRAB stand for and what is its cutoff?
back: Hypercalcemia — calcium greater than 11.5 mg/dL

subject: Hematology
front: What does the "R" in CRAB stand for and what is its cutoff?
back: Renal insufficiency — creatinine greater than 2 mg/dL, or creatinine clearance less than 40 mL/min

subject: Hematology
front: What does the "A" in CRAB stand for and what is its cutoff?
back: Anemia — hemoglobin less than 10 g/dL, or ≥2 g/dL below the normal value

subject: Hematology
front: What does the "B" in CRAB stand for and how is it detected?
back: Bone disease — one or more osteolytic lesions detected on X-ray, CT, MRI, or FDG-PET

subject: Hematology
front: What does the "S" stand for in the SLiM myeloma-defining biomarker criteria?
back: Sixty — 60% or more clonal plasma cells in the bone marrow

subject: Hematology
front: What does the "Li" stand for in the SLiM myeloma-defining biomarker criteria?
back: Light chain ratio — an involved/uninvolved serum free light chain ratio of 100 or more

subject: Hematology
front: What does the "M" stand for in the SLiM myeloma-defining biomarker criteria?
back: MRI lesions — more than 1 focal marrow lesion seen on MRI

subject: Hematology
front: Why does multiple myeloma cause purely osteolytic (not osteoblastic) lesions?
back: Due to osteoclast activation combined with suppression of osteoblasts, so no new bone formation occurs (reflected by reduced ALP and low tracer uptake)

subject: Hematology
front: What is seen on a bone scan (Tc-99m MDP) in multiple myeloma and why?
back: Cold spots, because there is no new bone formation/osteoblastic activity to take up the tracer

subject: Hematology
front: What are the classic skull X-ray lytic lesions of multiple myeloma called?
back: Punched-out lesions (also called raindrop lesions)

subject: Hematology
front: What causes rouleaux formation on peripheral smear in multiple myeloma?
back: Increased fibrinogen causing RBCs to clump together

subject: Hematology
front: What is the "protein gap" and what value suggests excess immunoglobulins?
back: Protein gap = Total protein minus Albumin; a gap greater than 4 g/dL suggests excess immunoglobulins

subject: Hematology
front: What are Bence-Jones proteins and what renal complication do they cause?
back: Free monoclonal light chains (kappa or lambda) found in urine; they cause light chain cast nephropathy

subject: Hematology
front: What is the prognostic significance of β2-microglobulin in multiple myeloma?
back: It is a prognostic marker reflecting tumor burden and renal function; a high β2-microglobulin indicates poor prognosis

subject: Hematology
front: What are the major causes of death in multiple myeloma?
back: Renal failure (from light chain cast nephropathy) and infections (very common)

subject: Hematology
front: What is the standard treatment regimen for multiple myeloma and their drug classes?
back: Bortezomib (proteasome inhibitor), Lenalidomide (immunomodulatory drug), and Dexamethasone

subject: Hematology
front: Which add-on drug targets CD38 in multiple myeloma treatment and how is a hypercalcemic crisis managed?
back: Daratumumab (anti-CD38 monoclonal antibody) is used as an add-on; hypercalcemic crisis is managed with IV hydration

subject: Hematology
front: What are Mott (Mulberry) cells and Russell bodies in multiple myeloma?
back: Mott/Mulberry cells are plasma cells containing multiple Russell bodies; Russell bodies are intracytoplasmic immunoglobulin inclusions

subject: Hematology
front: What are Dutcher bodies?
back: Intranuclear pseudoinclusions seen in plasma cells in multiple myeloma

subject: Hematology
front: What pattern is seen on serum protein electrophoresis in multiple myeloma and what commonly causes it?
back: An "M spike" (monoclonal spike), most commonly due to IgG

subject: Hematology
front: What is the typical serum protein electrophoresis pattern in Waldenström Macroglobulinemia?
back: Polyclonal (spread out) IgG with a monoclonal IgM and kappa spike

subject: Hematology
front: What is the "mini brain sign" on spinal MRI suggestive of?
back: A solitary plasmacytoma of the vertebra

subject: Hematology
front: Besides Mott/Mulberry cells, what other plasma cell morphologic variant is seen in multiple myeloma?
back: Flame cells (plasma cells with a fiery-red flaming cytoplasm, classically associated with IgA-producing myeloma)

subject: Hematology
front: What is the relative frequency order of immunoglobulin types causing the M-protein spike in multiple myeloma?
back: IgG > IgA > IgM > IgD > IgE (IgG is the most common, IgE the rarest)

subject: Hematology
front: What are the RBC, WBC, platelet, and JAK2 mutation findings in Polycythemia Vera?
back: RBC markedly increased (Hb >16 g/dL), WBC increased, platelets increased, JAK2 mutation present in >95% (drug: Ruxolitinib)

subject: Hematology
front: What are the RBC, WBC, platelet, and JAK2 mutation findings in Essential Thrombocytosis?
back: RBC and WBC normal, platelets markedly increased (>4.5 lakh/mm³), JAK2 mutation present in 30–50%

subject: Hematology
front: What are the RBC, WBC, platelet, and JAK2 mutation findings in CML?
back: RBC decreased, WBC markedly increased, platelets increased, JAK2 mutation absent

subject: Hematology
front: What are the RBC, WBC, platelet, and JAK2 mutation findings in Primary Myelofibrosis?
back: RBC decreased, WBC increased, platelets increased, JAK2 mutation present in 30–50%

subject: Hematology
front: What is relative polycythemia and what causes it?
back: Apparent polycythemia caused by decreased plasma volume (not true RBC mass increase)

subject: Hematology
front: What is primary polycythemia and its EPO status?
back: Polycythemia Vera; EPO levels are decreased

subject: Hematology
front: What is secondary polycythemia and its EPO status and causes?
back: EPO levels are increased due to hypoxia; causes include smoking, high altitude living, and being an athlete

subject: Hematology
front: Which is the most common myeloproliferative disorder and what pruritic symptom is it associated with?
back: Polycythemia Vera; associated with aquagenic pruritis, due to histamine release

subject: Hematology
front: What is the most common cause of death in Polycythemia Vera and its treatment?
back: Thrombosis is the most common cause of death; treatment is Ruxolitinib (a JAK2 inhibitor)

subject: Hematology
front: What symptom and bone marrow finding are associated with Essential Thrombocytosis?
back: Erythromelalgia (burning pain/redness in extremities) and staghorn megakaryocytes seen on histopathology

subject: Hematology
front: What are the three mechanisms that maintain hemostasis in the body?
back: Vascular spasm, platelet plug formation (primary hemostasis), and blood coagulation (secondary hemostasis)

subject: Hematology
front: What happens during vascular spasm after vessel injury?
back: Damaged blood vessels constrict

subject: Hematology
front: What happens during platelet plug formation and what type of hemostasis is this?
back: Circulating platelets gather at the site of endothelial injury and adhere to damaged endothelium to form a platelet plug; this is primary hemostasis

subject: Hematology
front: What happens during blood coagulation and what type of hemostasis is this?
back: Clots form via conversion of fibrinogen to fibrin through a series of steps known as the coagulation cascade; this is secondary hemostasis

subject: Hematology
front: What is the first response to endothelial injury and where is vWF stored before exposure?
back: Injury causes release of endothelin, producing transient vasoconstriction; vWF is stored in Weibel–Palade bodies of endothelial cells and becomes exposed upon injury

subject: Hematology
front: Which receptor mediates platelet adhesion to exposed vWF,  and what do platelets release upon adhesion?
back: Platelets bind vWF via the GpIb receptor, and release ADP, Ca2+, and TXA2

subject: Hematology
front: Which receptor mediates platelet activation and what receptor do activated platelets express?
back: ADP binds the P2Y12 receptor on platelets, causing activation; activated platelets then express GpIIb/IIIa receptors

subject: Hematology
front: Which molecule links platelets during platelet aggregation and via which receptor?
back: Fibrinogen binds GpIIb/IIIa receptors and links platelets together to form the platelet plug

subject: Hematology
front: Which platelet defect and disease results from loss of vWF?
back: Von Willebrand disease — a platelet adhesion defect

subject: Hematology
front: Which platelet defect and disease results from absent GpIb?
back: Bernard–Soulier syndrome — a platelet adhesion defect

subject: Hematology
front: Which platelet defect and disease results from absent GpIIb/IIIa?
back: Glanzmann thrombasthenia — a platelet aggregation defect

subject: Hematology
front: How do PGI2 (from endothelial cells) and TXA2 (from platelets) oppositely regulate platelet plug formation?
back: PGI2 (prostacyclin) inhibits platelet plug formation while TXA2 (thromboxane A2) promotes platelet plug formation

subject: Hematology
front: What are the four classes of antiplatelet drugs?
back: COX inhibitors, P2Y12 receptor blockers, GpIIb/IIIa inhibitors, and PAR-1 inhibitors

subject: Hematology
front: Which drug is the COX inhibitor antiplatelet agent?
back: Aspirin

subject: Hematology
front: Which P2Y12 receptor blockers are irreversible and which are reversible?
back: Irreversible: Ticlopidine, Clopidogrel, Prasugrel; Reversible: Ticagrelor, Cangrelor

subject: Hematology
front: Which GpIIb/IIIa inhibitors are monoclonal antibodies versus synthetic molecules?
back: Monoclonal antibody: Abciximab; Synthetic molecules: Eptifibatide, Tirofiban

subject: Hematology
front: What are the PAR-1 inhibitor antiplatelet drugs?
back: Atopaxar and Vorapaxar

subject: Hematology
front: How does Prasugrel compare to Clopidogrel in potency and what is a contraindication for it?
back: Prasugrel is 10 times more potent than clopidogrel; it is contraindicated in CVA/stroke patients because it is associated with severe bleeds

subject: Hematology
front: Why is Ticlopidine no longer used?
back: It carries a risk of neutropenia

subject: Hematology
front: What is notable about Abciximab and its safety profile?
back: It is a monoclonal antibody GpIIb/IIIa inhibitor that is safe to use in renal failure

subject: Hematology
front: What is the mechanism of action of Aspirin and how is its inhibition characterized?
back: Non-selective COX inhibitor that blocks formation of TXA2; produces irreversible ("hit-and-run"/suicide) inhibition, with effect persisting until new platelets are formed (about 8 days)

subject: Hematology
front: Which other drug class shares a similarly irreversible inhibition mechanism as Aspirin?
back: Proton pump inhibitors (PPIs)

subject: Hematology
front: What are the adverse effects of Aspirin at anti-inflammatory doses?
back: Gastric ulcer/GI bleeding, renal injury, Reye syndrome (microvesicular hepatic steatosis after viral infection in children), and respiratory alkalosis followed by HAGMA

subject: Hematology
front: Is Aspirin generally used in children, and what is the exception?
back: Aspirin is generally avoided in children, except in Kawasaki disease

subject: Hematology
front: What is dual antiplatelet therapy and which drug combinations are used?
back: Combination antiplatelet therapy using Aspirin plus Clopidogrel or Prasugrel

subject: Hematology
front: What triggers the intrinsic coagulation pathway and which factors are sequentially activated?
back: Damage to the endothelium triggers it; Factors 12, 11, and 9 are sequentially activated (mnemonic: T-E-N = Twelve, Eleven, Nine)

subject: Hematology
front: Which lab test evaluates the intrinsic coagulation pathway?
back: aPTT (Activated Partial Thromboplastin Time)

subject: Hematology
front: What triggers the extrinsic coagulation pathway and which factor is central to it?
back: Damage to tissues triggers it; Tissue factor (Factor 3) activates Factor 7

subject: Hematology
front: Which lab test evaluates the extrinsic coagulation pathway?
back: PT (Prothrombin Time)

subject: Hematology
front: What happens in the common coagulation pathway from Factor 10 onward?
back: Factor 10 is activated, then Factors 5, 2, and 1 are activated; Factor 1 (fibrinogen) is converted to fibrin, which forms a mesh stabilizing the platelet plug

subject: Hematology
front: What is the role of kallikrein in the intrinsic coagulation pathway and what else does it generate?
back: Kallikrein amplifies the intrinsic pathway by activating Factor XII; it also generates bradykinin, causing vasodilation and increased vascular permeability (relevant in Hereditary Angioedema, HAE)

subject: Hematology
front: What is unique about Factor 13 deficiency with respect to PT and aPTT?
back: It can cause coagulopathy despite normal PT and aPTT

subject: Hematology
front: Which coagulation factor has the shortest half-life and which has the longest?
back: Factor 7 has the shortest half-life; Factor 2 (prothrombin) has the longest half-life

subject: Hematology
front: Describe the fibrinolytic pathway from plasminogen to fibrin degradation products.
back: Plasminogen is converted to plasmin by tPA (tissue plasminogen activator); plasmin breaks down fibrin, producing fibrin degradation products (FDPs) such as D-Dimer

subject: Hematology
front: What is the mechanism of action of thrombolytic drugs and their indications?
back: They activate tPA; indicated in pulmonary embolism, ischemic cerebral stroke, and MI

subject: Hematology
front: What is the mnemonic SURAT for thrombolytic drugs?
back: Streptokinase, Urokinase, Reteplase, Alteplase, Tenecteplase

subject: Hematology
front: What is the mechanism of action of anti-thrombolytic (antifibrinolytic) drugs and their indications?
back: They block tPA; indicated in trauma and menorrhagia

subject: Hematology
front: Which two drugs are examples of anti-thrombolytics?
back: EACA (ε-aminocaproic acid) and Tranexamic acid (TXA)

subject: Hematology
front: What was the TXA dosing regimen used in the CRASH-2 trial and its patient population?
back: TXA 1 g IV over 10 minutes followed by 1 g IV over 8 hours, in trauma patients with significant bleeding

subject: Hematology
front: What do Protein C and Protein S inhibit as natural anticoagulants?
back: Factor V and Factor VIII

subject: Hematology
front: What is Factor V Leiden mutation and its significance?
back: The most common inherited thrombophilia; the mutation makes Factor V resistant to inactivation by Protein C

subject: Hematology
front: What does the molecular point mutation causing Factor V Leiden involve and what complications result?
back: A guanine to adenine DNA point mutation near the cleavage site, making Factor V resistant to degradation by activated Protein C; complications include DVT, cerebral vein thrombosis, and recurrent pregnancy loss

subject: Hematology
front: What does Antithrombin inhibit and how do Heparin/LMWH act on it?
back: Antithrombin inhibits Factor II (thrombin) and Factor X; Heparin and LMWH act by activating antithrombin

subject: Hematology
front: Does Warfarin activate antithrombin?
back: No, Warfarin does not activate antithrombin

subject: Hematology
front: Which coagulation factors are Vitamin K-dependent and how does Warfarin act on them?
back: Factors II, VII, IX, and X are Vitamin K-dependent; Warfarin inhibits their synthesis

subject: Hematology
front: What factor deficiencies cause Hemophilia A and Hemophilia B, and what is their inheritance?
back: Hemophilia A: deficiency of Factor VIII (X-linked); Hemophilia B: deficiency of Factor IX, also known as the Christmas factor (X-linked)

subject: Hematology
front: How are anticoagulant drugs broadly classified by route of administration?
back: Parenteral and Oral

subject: Hematology
front: How are parenteral anticoagulants further subdivided?
back: Indirect (Heparin: unfractionated heparin and LMWH) and Direct (Thrombin inhibitors: Hirudin, Bivalirudin, Argatroban; Factor Xa inhibitor: Otamixaban)

subject: Hematology
front: How are oral anticoagulants further subdivided?
back: Indirect (Warfarin/Dicoumarol) and Direct/DOACs (Thrombin inhibitor: Dabigatran; Factor Xa inhibitors: Rivaroxaban, Apixaban, Edoxaban)

subject: Hematology
front: What is the antidote for Dabigatran and for the oral Factor Xa inhibitors (Rivaroxaban/Apixaban/Edoxaban)?
back: Idarucizumab is the antidote for Dabigatran; Andexanet alfa is the antidote for the oral Factor Xa inhibitors

subject: Hematology
front: What is Ciraparantag and its mechanism?
back: A universal antidote for all DOACs, working against both Factor Xa inhibitors and direct thrombin inhibitors

subject: Hematology
front: What is the mechanism of action of unfractionated heparin (UFH) and its route of administration?
back: Activates antithrombin, indirectly inhibiting Factors 2 and X; administered IV or SC

subject: Hematology
front: Is unfractionated heparin safe in renal failure, and what monitoring does it require?
back: Yes, it is safe in renal failure; platelet monitoring is required due to risk of HIT

subject: Hematology
front: What is Heparin-Induced Thrombocytopenia (HIT) caused by, and what other adverse effects are associated with UFH?
back: HIT is caused by antibodies against platelet factor 4 (PF4); other UFH side effects include Type 4 RTA and osteopenia

subject: Hematology
front: What is the mechanism of action of LMWH, its route, and use in renal failure?
back: Inhibits Factor Xa more than Factor 2; administered only SC; cannot be used in renal failure; does not require monitoring

subject: Hematology
front: What are examples of LMWH and what is Fondaparinux?
back: Examples include Enoxaparin and Dalteparin; Fondaparinux is a synthetic heparin that acts only on Factor Xa

subject: Hematology
front: What is the drug of choice for DVT/PE/ACS and what bridging is required if starting Warfarin?
back: LMWH is the drug of choice; heparin bridging is required even when starting Warfarin

subject: Hematology
front: In what clinical situation is unfractionated heparin preferred over LMWH?
back: In renal failure, due to its short half-life and easy reversibility

subject: Hematology
front: What distinguishes Type 1 from Type 2 Heparin-Induced Thrombocytopenia (HIT)?
back: Type 1: mild, transient platelet drop, non-immune mediated; Type 2: immune-mediated (IgG-PF4 antibody), causes thrombocytopenia with thrombosis, and is serious (occurs in about 5% of heparin-exposed patients, Type 2 being more common clinically significant form)

subject: Hematology
front: What is the drug of choice for treating HIT and what should be avoided?
back: Argatroban or other direct thrombin inhibitors are the drug of choice; heparin and LMWH should be avoided

subject: Hematology
front: What is the antidote for heparin and LMWH?
back: Protamine sulfate

subject: Hematology
front: Which anticoagulant is safe in pregnancy and why is the alternative avoided?
back: LMWH is safe in pregnancy; Warfarin is avoided because it is teratogenic

subject: Hematology
front: What is the mechanism of action of Warfarin and which factors does it affect?
back: Blocks Vitamin K epoxide reductase; affects Vitamin K-dependent factors II, VII, IX, and X

subject: Hematology
front: How long does Warfarin take to achieve its effect and how is it monitored?
back: Takes 4–5 days to start effect; monitored using INR

subject: Hematology
front: Which enzyme metabolizes Warfarin and what other drug shares this pathway?
back: CYP2C9; Phenytoin is also metabolized via CYP2C9

subject: Hematology
front: What is purple toe syndrome, its cause, and how is it prevented?
back: A rare complication of Warfarin (presenting with dermal skin necrosis) caused by transient Protein C/S deficiency (initial procoagulant action of Warfarin); prevented by bridging Warfarin with heparin

subject: Hematology
front: In which condition is Warfarin the preferred anticoagulant, and what is a key contraindication?
back: Preferred in Atrial fibrillation; contraindicated in pregnancy due to teratogenicity

subject: Hematology
front: What is the antidote for Warfarin?
back: FFP, PCC (Prothrombin Complex Concentrate), or Vitamin K

subject: Hematology
front: What condition is associated with Purple Glove Syndrome and how does it differ from purple toe syndrome?
back: Purple Glove Syndrome is seen with Phenytoin, whereas purple toe syndrome is seen with Warfarin

subject: Hematology
